questions_and_answers.question_text: What does the pattern shéi...shéi jiù... mean?
Which adverb is often used in the main clause of this pattern?
Name four interrogative pronouns that can be used in this pattern.

answers.answer_text: Shéi, shénme, něige, nǎli (also zěnme, shénme shíhou, duōshǎo, and others).

questions_and_answers.question_text: What does -zhe show when added to an action verb like xiǎng?

answers.answer_text: The prolonging of the action over a period of time.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Is jiù always required in this pattern?

answers.answer_text: No — there are examples in which jiù is not used.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Translate into Chinese: I'll give you whatever you need.
Translate into Chinese: We'll meet wherever is most convenient for you.
Translate into English: Nǐ ài zěnmeyàng zěnmeyàng.
Write a Chinese sentence using -zhe to show a prolonged action.
Translate into Chinese: Whoever goes to China will always think of it.

articles.text:
12. A: Shéi qùguo Zhōngguó, shéi jiù huì xiǎngzhe ta.
   Whoever goes to China will always think of it.

Notes on No. 12

shéi...shéi jiù...: "whoever..." You can use an interrogative pronoun--shéi, shénme, něige, zěnme, nǎli, shénme shíhou, duōshǎo, etc.--in a dependent clause and then repeat it in the main clause to get meanings like "whoever," "whatever," "however," "wherever," "whenever," "however much," etc. The adverb jiù, "then," is often used in the main clause.

Nǐ xūyào shénme, wǒ jiù gěi nǐ shénme.
I'll give you whatever you need.

Nǎli duì nǐ zuì fāngbian wǒmen jiù zài nǎli jiàn miàn.
We'll meet wherever is most convenient for you.

Shéi xiǎng qù, shéi jiù qù.
Whoever wants to go, goes.

Here are some examples in which jiù is not used:

Nǐ ài zěnmeyàng zěnmeyàng.
Do whatever you like.

Nǐ shénme shíhou fāngbian, shénme shíhou lái.
Come whenever it's convenient for you.

Zài Táiwān, xiāngjiāo zǒngshi yǒu; yào duōshǎo, yǒu duōshǎo.
They always have bananas in Taiwan; there are as many as one could want (i.e., there are plenty).

xiǎngzhe: "be thinking of, have on one's mind" -Zhe on the end of an action verb like xiǎng shows the prolonging of the action over a period of time. Compare these examples:

Bié zhànzhe, zuòxia ba!
Don't stay standing; sit down!

Nǐ tīngzhe!
Listen!

Nǐ mànmàn chī, wǒ děngzhe nǐ.
Take your time eating; I'll wait for you.

Wǒ zài zhèr kānzhe ta, nǐ qù jiào liàng jiùhùchē.
I'll stay here and watch him; you go call an ambulance.
